title: Oedipus the King
author: Sophocles
tagline: The play in F. Storr’s verse translation, with one reader’s marginalia.
coverIntro: Below is the whole play, divided where a Greek tragedy divides itself: the prologue, the entry of the Chorus, then episodes with a choral ode after each, and the exodos. Each section is a landing on the trail. The faint arcs are where my notes reach across the play. Click a landing and start reading; lines underlined in red carry my notes, and each section ends with what I make of it.
crewIntro: The persons of the drama. Click a first appearance to go there.
about: This is the Project Gutenberg text of F. Storr’s translation, made for the Loeb Classical Library in 1912, unaltered. Storr put Sophocles into English blank verse with rhymed choruses, in an English that was already old-fashioned when he wrote it: “weird” for fate, “thou” throughout. It takes a page to tune the ear. The notes gloss the hard words.

The section titles are mine. The divisions are the play’s own; a Greek audience felt each one as the Chorus began to sing. There are {sections} sections here, with a reading of each and {notes} notes pinned to particular lines.

First performed around 429 BC. Everyone in the theatre knew how it ended before the first line was spoken, and the play is built on that knowledge. The notes assume the same, and point out the lines that mean more than their speaker knows.

movements.name: The Plague and the Vow
movements.desc: Oedipus swears to find the killer of Laius, curses him, and is told by Teiresias that he is the man, which nobody can believe.

movements.name: The Crossroads
movements.desc: A quarrel with Creon gives way to Jocasta's story of the three roads, and Oedipus begins to fear he killed the king.

movements.name: The Two Shepherds
movements.desc: News from Corinth turns the question from who killed Laius to who Oedipus is, and the herdsman answers it.

movements.name: The Open Doors
movements.desc: Jocasta's death and the blinding are reported, and Oedipus comes out to be seen, to judge himself, and to part from his daughters.

context.author: Sophocles (c. 496–406 BC) was a playwright and public figure in Athens. He competed in the city’s dramatic festivals and also served in political and military office. Seven of his tragedies survive complete.
context.world: Greek tragedy was a public experience, performed at festivals of Dionysus. Actors and a singing, dancing chorus brought heroic myths before an Athenian audience. Family obligations and civic authority could be debated in the same theatrical space.
